title: What data says about LEGO sets and their prices

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: What if you could look at decades of LEGO sets in one chart, and then check what a 1965 set sells for today?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Okay, I'm in. How do you even start?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Antoine collects LEGO and writes Python, so he combined two sources. Rebrickable's exports tell you what exists: sets, themes, parts and colors. A scraper on BrickEconomy tells you what people pay on the resale market.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Two trends. The number of sets released each year climbs steeply after the late nineties and passes a thousand in recent years. And the average part count per set rises from under a hundred in the seventies and eighties to around three hundred at the peak.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Star Wars leads by a wide margin, then Friends, Gear, Ninjago, Bionicle and Technic. He got there by counting sets per theme, joining the themes table and keeping the ten biggest top-level themes.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: And the scraper? Prices are on a web page, so that sounds easy.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Not quite. The price history isn't in an HTML table. It sits in an inline script that feeds a Google Charts table, so his parser reads the script tags and pulls the rows out. He built it with Playwright and async Python.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Think of it as reading the stage directions instead of watching the play.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Ha, right. For the test case he picked set 001-1, the 1965 Samsonite Gears set, with a long history and enough resale activity to plot. The scraper writes two files: dated values with annotations like the release, and monthly ranges for sealed copies.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Then he cleaned it and fit a model?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Yes. Pandas removes duplicates, strips currency symbols and parses dates. Then a plain linear regression of value against date, projected to 2030, gives a simple trend line to ask questions of: where do the recent spikes sit against it?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: LEGO data is a friendly way to practice pandas, async scraping and charting. The full write-up has every chart, and the code lives in the LegosTracker repository.
